lesson.menu_title: The Board-Ready Mind -- Modal Perfects for Strategic Retrospection
lesson.menu_desc: A gramatica do post-mortem: should have, could have, must have -- e por que cinco should have viram autoflagelo
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 11 -- The Board-Ready Mind
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Denise Gadelha Rocha | Lesson 11 -- The Board-Ready Mind

listenings.text: I ran reviews for eleven years, and almost all of the bad ones fail in the same place. They start with who, and the who arrives before the what. Once a name is on the table, everybody in the room is defending something, and the analysis is over. The good ones invert it. They rebuild the timeline first, what was known on the fourteenth of June and by whom, before anybody is allowed to say what should have happened. Hindsight makes the signal look enormous. At the time it was one line in a report of forty. The second thing I watch for is the language. If somebody tells me the market must have shifted, I ask what would be true if it had. If they cannot answer, they are not deducing, they are decorating. And the last rule is mine. A review that ends without a date and a name has not ended. It has been postponed.

There is a version of accountability that is really just anxiety, and I did it for years. I would open a review by listing everything I should have done, on the theory that if I said it first, nobody else could say it to me. It works exactly once. After that the room does not hear ownership. It hears somebody who cannot stop apologising, and quietly it stops giving that person difficult work to do. What changed it for me was one line from a chairman. Say it once, say it in the past, and then talk about October. One sentence of should have, and everything after that in the future. The other habit I had to lose was second-guessing in public, reopening the same decision three times in one meeting. In retrospect is a useful phrase. Said four times in ten minutes, it is a person negotiating with the past in front of an audience.

extra_audio.text: Revenue closed four points below plan, and the shortfall sits almost entirely in the industrial book. The warning sign was there in June, and the pressure must have been building since March. The root cause was an assumption about the renewal cycle that nobody owned, so nobody tested it. From October we re-price the twenty largest accounts every month, and that review has my name against it.
